Needs block_linear, ScaleShiftMACE and a factored last interaction (MH-1, OMOL-0). fold_product_linear auto, on, off On with species_tables and block_linear where the model takes it, in plans that are not reproducible. Folds layer 0's product linear into the linear layers that read layer 0's output, with the species carried next to the contraction. rounding, deterministic. Needs block_linear and species_tables.

docs.title: Compiler (Inductor)
docs.text:
These change how torch.compile builds the model. They have no effect when nothing is compiled (EngineConfig.compile_mode="none").

Option Values Default (auto means) What it does Exactness / limits combo_kernels auto, on, off Off. Only "on" enables it. Turns on Inductor's combo kernels for pointwise operations: independent adjacent pointwise kernels run in one launch. rounding (the energy moves by about 1e-9 relative), deterministic. save_transcendentals auto, on, off On only in float64 MH-1 plans that are not reproducible, on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti or an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada Generation. Off elsewhere. A custom partitioner saves the results of transcendental operations (exp, tanh, sigmoid and others) for the backward pass instead of recomputing them there. exact, deterministic. May use more memory, since the saved tensors are kept until the backward.

docs.title: Precision tricks
docs.text:
Option Values Default (auto means) What it does Exactness / limits tf32x3_gemms auto, on, off Off. Only "on" enables it. Runs every atom-level matrix product (block linears, segment_gemm, species skip, reassociated first interaction) and its input gradient as three TF32 tensor-core products (Triton's tf32x3), which together reach about float32 accuracy. rounding, deterministic; not equivalent to IEEE float32 when terms cancel. Needs block_linear, float32 and compute capability 8.0 or higher. Conflicts with grouped_launch: set grouped_launch="off" with it on the generic MACE family.

The float64 emulation on integer tensor cores, and its mantissa bits, are engine options (EngineConfig.fp64_emulation, EngineConfig.fp64_emulation_mantissa_bits), not rewrites.

docs.title: PolarMACE
docs.text:
These apply only to MACE-POLAR-1 models.

Option Values Default (auto means) What it does Exactness / limits polar_uvu True, False (bool) True. No effect on other models. Reassociates PolarMACE's sparse UVU tensor product (the l × l → 0 paths contract the weight first, as one matrix product) instead of forming the pair tensor. rounding, deterministic. fx_e3nn_linear auto, on, off On for the checkpoints polar1-s, polar1-m and polar1-l (identified by SHA-256) in hybrid float32 plans that are not reproducible. Off for every other model. Builds e3nn's o3.Linear as an fx graph instead of the TorchScript a checkpoint restores, so the compiler can trace PolarMACE's whole forward. rounding, deterministic. polar_graph_sums auto, on, off As fx_e3nn_linear. Computes PolarMACE's per-structure sums (Fukui norms, total charges, barycentre) as a sum over atoms and a broadcast, not with scatter_add_ and an index. rounding, deterministic (no atomics). Needs one structure per evaluation, which is always the case.

docs.title: Stress
docs.text: Option Values Default (auto means) What it does Exactness / limits single_graph_strain auto, on, off On for every engine. It acts only where stress is computed (variable-cell MD, relaxations with a cell filter). Uses MACE PR 1498's one-structure strain: the strained cell is used directly instead of being gathered per edge. Bound into the force field's own forward; nothing in MACE is patched process-wide. rounding, deterministic. Needs one structure per evaluation.

docs.title: PrecisionConfig
docs.text:
The force evaluation runs in float32 or float64. Integration is always float64: positions, momenta, thermostat and barostat state are float64 whatever the force precision. The potential energy is summed in float64 in both precisions.

Float32 is the default and the fast path: several rewrites (segment_gemm, grouped_launch, fused_folded_forward, wprime_backward, tf32x3_gemms, the PolarMACE compiler rewrites) are float32 only. Float64 is slower; how much depends on the GPU's float64 rate. Choose float64 when:

  • you need energies or forces beyond float32 rounding, for example for finite-difference checks or long NVE runs where float32 drift matters;
  • you compare against a float64 reference or another float64 code;
  • the gate (check="gate") fails in float32 on your system.

On GPUs with a reduced float64 rate (consumer and workstation cards, about 1/64 of float32) the planner turns on cuBLAS's float64 emulation on integer tensor cores (EngineConfig.fp64_emulation), which keeps float64 accuracy.

Not every field is set through PrecisionConfig by users. The table says where each one comes from.

Option Values Default (auto means) What it does Exactness / limits dtype auto, float32, float64 Set with fm.ForceField(model, atoms, precision=...) (default "float32"); fm.md always uses float32. The planner's own "auto" rule (float32 for the hybrid backend, float64 for plain cuEq) is not used for user plans: the planner takes the force field's precision. Precision of the model and of the force evaluation. On a MACE install whose float64-energy patch cannot be applied (its source hash does not match), a non-PolarMACE float32 force field is promoted to float64, so the energy is still summed in float64. The plan records this as the force_precision decision. tf32 False, True (bool) False. Not settable through Simulation, fm.md or ForceField. TF32 tensor-core matrix products. Never on by default. True is only a label in the plan ("TF32" in the header); FastMACE never switches PyTorch's TF32 mode. metadata.json records the real flag as precision.tf32 and this field as precision.tf32_requested. If your script enables TF32 (torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")), float32 forces are no longer IEEE float32. float64_energy True, False (bool) True. Not settable through Simulation, fm.md or ForceField. Accumulates the potential energy in float64 (forces and stress are MACE's either way). False reproduces the research engine's float32 energy sum, for A/B comparisons only. mc_energy auto, float32, float64 Set with fm.Workload(mc_energy_precision=...). "auto": the force precision if the move-energy gate passes, float64 otherwise. Without MC moves it equals the force precision. Precision of the energies that Monte Carlo moves compare. MD forces keep dtype. "float32" with float64 forces is refused: MC energies are never evaluated below the force precision.

docs.title: When to change these
docs.text:
You almost never need to. The "auto" rules come from same-process A/B timings and force gates, and every rewrite is checked when it is applied. Leave rewrites="auto" unless one of these applies.

To bisect a gate failure or a suspicious result. Turn rewrites off one at a time, or a whole chain at its root (factor_species="off" or block_linear="off"), and compare. The automatic fallback after a failed gate does the same search and records it in sim.gate. Simulation(mode="reference") runs with no rewrites at all.

To try the opt-in rewrites. These are off under "auto" because they gave no gain, or a loss, in the measurements so far:

Option Measured direct_node_feats, folded_constants Together, NaCl about 0.5–1 % faster on an RTX 5060 Ti; NbCl5 and an L4 neutral. combo_kernels NaCl about 1–2 % faster, NbCl5 2–3 % slower on an RTX 5060 Ti and an L4. fused_radial_hidden No measured gain. tf32x3_gemms An accuracy screen; slower than cuBLAS float32 on most production shapes measured. gate_epilogue MH-1 with wprime_backward on (the default on both GPUs): no gain; NbCl5 0.3 % slower on an RTX 4000 Ada, NaNbO3 0.7-0.9 % slower on an RTX 5060 Ti. Small cells such as NaCl run the stock path.

Test them with a same-process A/B on your own GPU and structure before you rely on them.

Float64 on other GPUs. w_tables and save_transcendentals are on only on the two GPU models where they were measured faster in float64 MH-1 runs (an RTX 5060 Ti and an RTX 4000 Ada): per MD step w_tables 0.86–0.94 and save_transcendentals 0.97–0.98 of the time without them. On an A100, which runs float64 at half the float32 rate, both were slower (w_tables 1.06–1.27, save_transcendentals up to 1.02). On another reduced-rate GPU you may set them "on" and measure. Unmeasured GPUs keep them off even when they share a compute capability with a measured one.

For reproducible plans. With fm.Workload(reproducible=True) the planner uses plain cuEq and turns off every rewrite that is not deterministic or that is kept for non-reproducible plans only (radial_tables, species_tables, fold_readout_tail, fold_product_linear, segment_gemm, grouped_launch, fused_folded_forward, w_tables, wprime_backward, save_transcendentals, fx_e3nn_linear, polar_graph_sums). An explicit "on" for a rewrite that is not deterministic is refused.

To save memory. radial_tables and w_tables hold tables that grow with the square of the species count. Turn them off if the plan's memory estimate is close to the GPU's memory.

docs.title: Prebuilt OEq host-extension wheels: fastmace-oeq-ext (plan task 6-T04)
docs.text: Owner decisions (plans/phase-6.md): D3 (a) torch 2.14.1+cu130 only; D4 (a) prebuilt wheels on PyPI as a separate package fastmace-oeq-ext, Linux x86_64, CPython 3.10 to 3.13.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
OpenEquivariance 0.7.0 builds a small C++ host extension (libtorch_tp_jit.so, pybind11 plus TORCH_LIBRARY ops) with torch.utils.cpp_extension.load at its first import, which needs g++ and ninja (oeq-runtime.md). Its device kernels are compiled with NVRTC at run time, so the host library is the only compiled part. fastmace-oeq-ext ships that library, built from OEq's unmodified sources against torch 2.14.1+cu130, one wheel per CPython:

Wheel Tag Contents fastmace_oeq_ext-0.7.0.post1-cp310-cp310-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl cp310 fastmace_oeq_ext/{__init__.py, libtorch_tp_jit.so, manifest.json, LICENSE.openequivariance, BUILD_COMPILER.txt} ...-cp311-cp311-... / ...-cp312-cp312-... cp311 / cp312 the same ...-cp313-cp313-... cp313 the same; Python 3.13 support added by 6-T15

dependencies = ["torch==2.14.1", "openequivariance==0.7.0"]. Licence MIT AND BSD-3-Clause: the packaging is FastMACE's MIT, the library OEq's BSD-3 (its licence ships in the wheel, as BSD-3 clause 2 requires for binaries). The version 0.7.0.postN follows OEq's; N counts rebuilds.

The library links libc10/libtorch*/libtorch_python (found through $ORIGIN/../torch/lib) and libcudart/libnvrtc/libcublas.so.13 ($ORIGIN/../nvidia/cu13/lib, the wheels torch already loads), and libcuda.so.1 from the driver. It does not link libpython (OEq's JIT build does, for its AOTI path only).

docs.title: How FastMACE picks it
docs.text:
fastmace.kernels._oeq_runtime.prebuilt_extension() reads fastmace_oeq_ext/manifest.json without importing anything and accepts it only if torch (with its +cu130 tag), OpenEquivariance and the CPython tag match exactly, the platform is Linux x86_64 and the library exists. Then prepare_in_process sets up the stand-in CUDA home as before (links only), and wraps torch.utils.cpp_extension.load so that OEq's load_jit_extension("libtorch_tp_jit", ...) gets the prebuilt module; nothing is compiled and no build cache is written. Otherwise it builds with the host toolchain, as before, and records why the wheel was not used (extension["prebuilt_skipped"]).

  • FASTMACE_OEQ_PREBUILT=0: never use the wheel. =1: refuse to build (the clean-install check uses it).
  • fastmace doctor prints host extension: prebuilt (fastmace-oeq-ext 0.7.0.post1, <path>); no compiler needed, or built with the host toolchain ...; prebuilt not used: <reason>, and only then requires g++ and ninja.
  • The run's patch record oeq_runtime (provenance, metadata.json) ends with host extension: prebuilt (<path>) or host extension: built|reused|raced|in-process.

pip install "fastmace[oeq]" pulls fastmace-oeq-ext with the marker sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'x86_64' and python_version < '3.14'. On another torch pip refuses to resolve (torch==2.14.1 pin); install openequivariance alone to use the toolchain build.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
tools/release/oeq_wheels/build.sh ~/tmp/6-T04/wheels    # WSL or Linux; docker or Docker Desktop's docker.exe

build.sh streams this directory into quay.io/pypa/manylinux_2_28_x86_64 (gcc-toolset 14) and runs build_in_container.sh: pinned CUDA 13 header/library wheels (runtime 13.0.96, nvrtc 13.0.88, crt 13.0.88, cccl 13.0.85, cublas 13.1.1.3, as torch 2.14.1+cu130 requires), torch 2.14.1+cu130 and pybind11 3.1.0 per Python, the two OEq sources compiled with the flags of OEq's own JIT build, a stub libcuda.so for the link, strip, then a py3-none-any wheel retagged cpXY-cpXY-manylinux_2_28_x86_64. Scratch lives in the docker volume fastmace-oeq-ext-work, wheels come out through fastmace-oeq-ext-out; nothing touches the repository. Docker Desktop's WSL integration was off on the PC, so DOCKER=docker.exe (the Windows client) was used.

Nothing is uploaded. Publishing is the owner's step: twine check then twine upload of the three wheels.

docs.title: Clean-install check
docs.text: tools/release/clean_install.sh WHEEL_DIR [PYTHON] makes a fresh uv venv under ~/tmp/6-T04, installs torch 2.14.1+cu130, cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu13 and fastmace[oeq] from the checkout with the local wheels (--find-links), then shadows g++, c++, ninja and nvcc with sentinels that log and fail, sets FASTMACE_OEQ_PREBUILT=1, runs fastmace doctor and a 20-step NaCl (64 atoms, MH-1) NVT smoke, and requires the hybrid backend, a prebuilt host extension and an empty sentinel log. gcc (C) stays on PATH: Triton compiles its CUDA launcher stub with a C compiler, a separate requirement (6-T03). Run it under the local reservation: python3 tools/ci/local_gpu.py run --purpose ... -- bash tools/release/clean_install.sh DIR.

docs.title: How the patches were made and what was verified (25 October 2026)
docs.text:
The upstream repositories were not cloned. The files each patch touches were fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at the commits above into scratch git repositories, edited there, and diffed. The new modules were then run against the installed packages on the local PC (WSL2, RTX 5060 Ti), which are older than upstream main:

Patch Run against Result MACE block linear fastmace_cpu venv: MACE 0.3.16, cuEquivariance 0.13.0, torch 2.14.1+cpu; the new module loaded from the patch, tests/unit/test_block_linear.py 13 passed (with the reassociation tests: 19 passed, run_mace_tests.py) MACE reassociation same venv; tests/unit/test_reassociate.py builds small float64 MACE models (Residual, DensityResidual, ResidualNonLinear first blocks) and compares energy and forces 6 passed OEq wheel build tests/wheel_cuda_test.py in mace_cueq_latest: 3 passed, 1 skipped (the end-to-end test needs OEQ_TEST_WHEEL_BUILD=1). check_wheel_build.py in mace_cueq_oeq (OEq 0.7.0, torch 2.14.1+cu130): built OEq 0.7.0's host-extension sources with only the patch's flags, CUDA_HOME/CUDA_PATH unset and no nvcc on PATH, in 18–20 s; the library loaded and ldd resolved cudart, nvrtc, cublas to the nvidia/cu13 wheel and libcuda.so.1 to the driver pass

Not verified:

  • the patches applied to and tested inside the upstream trees (MACE main has dropped Python 3.10; our environments are Python 3.10, so MACE main's test suite was not run). The MACE patches only add new files and do not touch existing ones, so they apply to e37c858 by construction; the OEq patch was diffed against dc99790's extlib/__init__.py, which differs from 0.7.0's (SYCL backend), and its edited branch was exercised only through check_wheel_build.py, not by importing the patched openequivariance package;

run_mace_tests.py is the small runner used for the MACE tests (it loads the new modules from the patch files into an installed MACE 0.3.16).

docs.title: MACE PR draft: block and grouped linear for cuEquivariance Linear
docs.text: Upstream: ACEsuit/mace, base main at e37c8583a8b1b586e5888fa6dca86e8f591e2606 (merge of develop, 19 October 2026). Patch: 0001-block-linear.patch (new files only: mace/modules/block_linear.py, tests/unit/test_block_linear.py). Not opened (owner opens it, decision D5 (b)).

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Add an inference-time block-linear conversion for cuEquivariance Linear layers (per-l GEMMs, 2–12 % faster MD steps)

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
With enable_cueq=True, every equivariant linear layer of MACE is a cuet.Linear(method="naive") (mace/modules/wrapper_ops.py, Linear.__new__). For inference the weights are constant, and such a layer is block-diagonal: each input segment mul_in x ir maps to each output segment of the same irrep through one [mul_in, mul_out] matrix, applied alike to all 2l + 1 components. It can therefore run as one plain GEMM per (input segment, output segment) on [n * (2l + 1), mul] rows of the ir_mul layout.

This PR adds mace.modules.block_linear.convert_block_linears(model, grouped=True), an opt-in, inference-only conversion that:

  1. extracts each layer's effective weights from the module itself (linear.f on a unit basis), so path normalisation and layout are cuEquivariance's own and not re-derived;
  2. multiplies the input gradient (forces) by a precomputed contiguous transposed weight. The autograd backward otherwise multiplies by a transposed view, and cuBLAS picks slower kernels for it (15–25 % slower on MACE-MH-1's 512 x 512 blocks);
  3. with grouped=True (default) concatenates the same-irrep input segments that feed one output segment (the linear after the convolution: several 128x1o paths into one block) and multiplies them by their stacked weights in one GEMM, instead of one GEMM per path plus additions of wide outputs.

Nothing changes for training or for users who do not call the conversion.

docs.title: Measured gains (from our validation reports; same algorithm, FastMACE/research-engine implementation)
docs.text:
All MD-step timings are float32, cuEquivariance/OpenEquivariance hybrid, CUDA graphs, MACE-MH-1, 3x3x3 supercells, same-process A/B.

Change NaCl (216 atoms) NaNbO3 NbCl5 GPU Source block linear alone (per-l GEMMs + contiguous transposed backward) −11.8 % −1.5 % −0.9 % RTX 5060 Ti ResearchModule Experiments/Langevin_Thermostat/docs/roadmap.md item 12, 14 October 2026 grouped + merged residual (on top) −3.5 to −4.6 % −2.3 to −2.9 % −4.2 % RTX 4000 Ada (murphy) same, item 12, 16 October 2026; studies/other_models/README.md

Both passed the force-gate check (float32 force error against float64 at most 2x that of the stock float32 calculator) and the CUDA-graph replay gate. FastMACE carries them as registry records block_linear, grouped_linear (fastmace/rewrites/linear/), default on; see docs/rewrites.md.

The merged residual (one product per output segment over linear_1(message) and linear_res(linear_up(x)) of the MH-1-class RealAgnosticResidualNonLinearInteractionBlock) is not in this patch: it needs the interaction forward to divide by the density before linear_1, which is a separate change. It could follow as a second PR.

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text: Same terms, different summation order: exact up to floating-point rounding. In float64 the test agrees with cuet.Linear to 1e-12 (values and input gradients). Deterministic (no atomics).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• inference only: weights are frozen buffers, gradients with respect to them are not computed;
  • not TorchScript/LAMMPS-exportable (custom autograd function); convert after export;
  • only cuet.Linear with internal shared weights and one weight class; others are left unchanged.

docs.title: Test plan
docs.text:
• [x] tests/unit/test_block_linear.py: float64, mul_ir and ir_mul, grouped and ungrouped, three irreps patterns (MH-1-like 128→512, repeated input irrep, output irrep without input) against cuet.Linear, values and input gradients; non-cuEq modules untouched. Run: 13 passed on MACE 0.3.16 / cuEquivariance 0.13.0 / torch 2.14.1+cpu (not on MACE main, which needs Python ≥ 3.11).
  • [ ] maintainers' CI on main (Python 3.11–3.14).
  • [ ] GPU: energy/forces of a converted mace-mp-0 medium vs unconverted, float32 and float64, and an MD-step timing (tests/benchmarks), to reproduce the table above with this plain-PyTorch version.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Gain depends on shapes and GPU. The 11.8 % on NaCl is small-system; large cells gain ~1 %. Expect smaller gains without CUDA graphs (launch overhead dominates small systems).
  • Weight extraction relies on linear.f([weight, x]) being cuEquivariance's polynomial call. If cuEquivariance changes that internal API, the conversion fails loudly (no silent wrong values), and the unit test catches it.
  • Memory: one extra transposed copy of every weight (a few MB for MH-1).
  • Users may forget the model is frozen; the docstring and the function name say so.

docs.title: MACE PR draft: reassociated first interaction
docs.text: Upstream: ACEsuit/mace, base main at e37c8583a8b1b586e5888fa6dca86e8f591e2606 (19 October 2026). Patch: 0001-reassociate-first.patch (new files only: mace/modules/reassociate.py, tests/unit/test_reassociate.py). Not opened (owner opens it, decision D5 (b)).

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Add an inference-time reassociation of the first interaction: sum edges per (receiver, sender species) before the radial projection

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
In the first interaction block the sender features are species-only scalars (linear_up(node_embedding(one_hot))), and the convolution is channelwise with one radial weight per (path, channel). Today every edge forms its [P*C] tensor-product weights (conv_tp_weights, e.g. 4 x 128 = 512 values per edge) and the tensor product, then sums per receiver. Because the last radial layer is affine and the sender features depend only on the sender's species, the sums can be reassociated:

m[i, l, m, u] = gamma_l  sum_z x[z, u]  sum_k W[path(l)·C + u, k]  S[i, z, k, (l, m)]
S[i, z, k, (l, m)] = sum_{edges j→i, species(j)=z}  a[e, k] Y[e, (l, m)],     a[e] = [h_e c_e, c_e]

S is a small edge sum over K ≈ 65 hidden radial features (plus a bias column), and the projection is one dense GEMM per path over [atoms·(2l+1), species·K]. The per-edge weights are never formed.

The conversion reassociate_first_interaction(model, species_columns=None) needs no change to any interaction forward: it swaps conv_tp_weights for "hidden layers, then append a 1 column" (the forward's existing * cutoff produces a), and conv_tp for a module with the fused calling convention (conv_fusion), which gets node_attrs from a forward pre-hook. gamma_l and the output layout are measured from the model's own conv_tp (e3nn, cuEquivariance or OpenEquivariance), so no normalisation convention is assumed. The conversion returns False and leaves the model unchanged where the form does not hold (non-scalar sender irreps, non-channelwise TP, non-affine last radial layer, models with joint_embedding).

docs.title: Measured gains (FastMACE / research-engine implementation of the same algorithm)
docs.text:
Model Change NaCl NaNbO3 NbCl5 GPU Source MACE-MH-1 plain PyTorch prototype (as in this patch) −0.6 to −2.6 % RTX 5060 Ti ResearchModule docs/roadmap.md item 11.2, 10 October 2026 MACE-MH-1 with a fused Triton backward of the edge sum −4.9 % −7.2 % −4.9 % RTX 5060 Ti same MP-0, MPA-0, OMAT-0, MatPES and other non-MH-1 benchmark models with the receiver-streaming convolution, together −16 to −28 % RTX 5060 Ti docs/roadmap.md item 13, studies/other_models/README.md, 15 October 2026 MACE-OMOL-0 reassociation added −9 % RTX 5060 Ti AGENTS.md / studies/other_models/README.md, 16 October 2026

MD-step times, float32 hybrid, CUDA graphs, 3x3x3 cells. All passed the force and graph-replay gates. FastMACE: records reassociate_first (MH-1 family, fastmace/rewrites/mh1/) and generic_reassociate (fastmace/rewrites/generic/); float64 agreement 1.3e-16 to 3.2e-15 eV/Å on mp0-medium (docs/validation/1a-T08-generic-rewrites.md). Its edge-sum cost after the rewrite is 0.06 ms (NaCl) to 0.5 ms (NbCl5) per force call (docs/validation/2-T20a-step-breakdown.md).

Honest expectation for this patch: it is the plain PyTorch form (an index_add_ of outer products, autograd backward). Our measurements say most of the gain needs a fused backward of the edge sum; this PR is the correct, general base on which such a kernel can be added later.

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text: The same products in a different summation order: exact up to rounding. The float64 test agrees with the unconverted model to 1e-10 eV (energy) and 1e-9 eV/Å (forces) on Residual, DensityResidual and ResidualNonLinear first blocks. index_add_ on CUDA uses atomics: not bitwise reproducible on GPU (as MACE's scatter_sum already is).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• inference only (weights frozen into a buffer);
  • memory of S is atoms x species x (lmax+1)^2 x (K+1); pass species_columns (the elements a simulation can contain) for 89-element foundation models;
  • the converted model is not TorchScript-exportable (forward pre-hook with kwargs, Python state);
  • the species table x is read back from node_feats with index_reduce_(amax), which assumes that every atom of a species has identical first-layer features (true for species-only embeddings; models with joint_embedding are refused).

docs.title: Test plan
docs.text:
• [x] tests/unit/test_reassociate.py: float64 three-species MACE models with each residual first block, energy and forces against the unconverted model, with and without species_columns. Run: 6 passed on MACE 0.3.16 / torch 2.14.1+cpu (MACE main itself not run: Python 3.10 environment).
  • [ ] maintainers' CI on main.
  • [ ] GPU: mace-mp-0 medium and MH-1 with enable_cueq and enable_oeq (the conv_fusion probe path), float32 force check, MD-step timing.
  • [ ] a model whose conv_tp_weights is e3nn's FullyConnectedNet with normalised weights (affinity probe covers it; add an explicit test).

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Small or no gain without a fused backward, as measured (0.6–2.6 %). Reviewers may prefer to wait for a kernel.
  • Probing relies on internal structure (interaction.edge_irreps, edge_attrs_irreps, conv_tp.weight_numel, radial net layer list). Any mismatch returns False rather than producing wrong numbers, and the affinity of the last radial layer is checked numerically.
  • Pre-hook state (conv_tp.node_attrs) is per call; concurrent calls of one model object from two threads would race (MACE does not do this).

docs.title: OpenEquivariance PR draft: build the JIT host extension from the NVIDIA runtime wheels (no toolkit, no nvcc)
docs.text: Upstream: PASSIONLab/OpenEquivariance, base main at dc9979099c65113adcc016977c5c60974f9ddafb (27 September 2026, after v0.7.0). Patch: 0001-wheel-cuda-host-build.patch: edits openequivariance/openequivariance/_torch/extlib/__init__.py, adds .../extlib/wheel_cuda.py and tests/wheel_cuda_test.py. Not opened (owner opens it, decision D5 (b)).

docs.title: Title
docs.text: JIT extension: build against the pip NVIDIA CUDA wheels when no CUDA toolkit is installed

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The torch host extension libtorch_tp_jit has only C++ sources; its device kernels are compiled at run time with NVRTC. Building it needs the CUDA runtime headers and link libraries, not nvcc. A PyTorch install from PyPI already ships both in the NVIDIA wheels (nvidia/cu13/{include,lib} for CUDA 13; nvidia/cuda_runtime, cuda_nvrtc, cublas, cuda_cccl for CUDA 12). But load_jit_extension() calls include_paths("cuda") and library_paths("cuda"), which require torch.utils.cpp_extension.CUDA_HOME. On machines without a toolkit (shared HPC workstations, cloud images, Colab-like VMs, containers built from python: images) CUDA_HOME is None, the build fails, and MACE silently runs without OEq. Where the precompiled extension does not apply (torch < 2.10, OEQ_JIT_EXTENSION=1, HIP), users currently need a toolkit or a wrapper script that fakes one.

We ran OEq 0.7 on toolkit-less workstations for weeks through such a wrapper (a directory of symbolic links standing in for CUDA_HOME, plus an nvcc sentinel that fails loudly), later replaced by in-process preparation in FastMACE (fastmace/kernels/_oeq_runtime.py; findings in docs/design/oeq-runtime.md). The sentinel was never invoked: no step of the build needs nvcc. This PR removes the need for any such wrapper.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
• new extlib/wheel_cuda.py: wheel_build_flags() finds the wheel directories in site-packages and returns explicit include directories (with CCCL) and linker arguments that link each library by soname (-l:libcudart.so.13, -l:libnvrtc.so.13, -l:libcublas.so.13, driver -l:libcuda.so.1) with an RPATH to the wheel. No CUDA_HOME and no unversioned lib*.so links are needed. The driver directory is searched in the usual places (/usr/lib/wsl/lib, multiarch, /usr/lib64, /usr/lib64-nvidia) or taken from OEQ_CUDA_DRIVER_DIR.
  • load_jit_extension() (CUDA branch only): new variable OEQ_CUDA_FROM_WHEELS = auto (default: wheels only when CUDA_HOME is None, so existing toolkit builds are unchanged), 1 (always; error if the wheels are missing), 0 (never). With the wheels, the device include path is include_paths("cpu") plus the wheel's.
  • HIP and SYCL branches untouched.

docs.title: Why linking by soname matters
docs.text: On one of our workstations the libpython directory (/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu) also holds a system CUDA 11.5's development links (libnvrtc.so, libcudart.so). OEq passes -L<libpython dir> before the CUDA directories, so -lnvrtc resolved to CUDA 11 and the extension mixed runtimes. -l:libnvrtc.so.13 plus -L<wheel> cannot pick a different major version.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Local PC, WSL2, RTX 5060 Ti, torch 2.14.1+cu130, OEq 0.7.0, nvidia-cuda-runtime 13.0.96, g++ 13.3: check_wheel_build.py (in this folder) builds OEq 0.7.0's host sources with only the new flags, CUDA_HOME/CUDA_PATH unset, no nvcc on PATH: built in 18–20 s, loaded with torch.ops.load_library, and ldd shows libcudart.so.13, libnvrtc.so.13, libcublas.so.13 (and libcublasLt.so.13) from nvidia/cu13/lib and libcuda.so.1 from the driver.
  • The equivalent symbolic-link layout (same headers, same libraries) has built and run OEq 0.7.0 with MACE on four workstations (RTX A4000, RTX 4000 Ada x2, RTX 5060 Ti) since 8 October 2026; forces of the in-process route agree with the wrapper-script route to 3.9e-7 eV/Å, the same scatter as two runs of the script itself (docs/design/oeq-runtime.md, run table).

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text: Build-system change only; the compiled code is the same. No effect on kernels.

docs.title: Test plan
docs.text:
• [x] tests/wheel_cuda_test.py (CPU, no GPU): cu13 layout found and flags correct (CCCL include, sonames, one -L per directory, driver last); missing wheel and missing library return None. Run: 3 passed, 1 skipped (in torch 2.14.1+cu130, Python 3.10).
  • [x] build check on a toolkit-less configuration (above), with OEq 0.7.0 sources and the flags this patch computes.
  • [ ] OEQ_TEST_WHEEL_BUILD=1 pytest tests/wheel_cuda_test.py on a GPU host with the patched package (imports openequivariance._torch.extlib in a subprocess without CUDA_HOME). Not run: we did not install the patched upstream main.
  • [ ] verify_extension_build.yml: add a job leg on a runner image without the CUDA toolkit.
  • [ ] CUDA 12 wheels (torch==2.x+cu126): untested; the code path exists.
  • [ ] then tests/conv_test.py / batch_test.py with the wheel-built extension.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• auto changes behaviour only where the build failed before (CUDA_HOME is None); with a toolkit the old path runs. Users with a toolkit and wheels keep the toolkit (set =1 to prefer the wheels).
  • Header/runtime skew: the wheel's headers match the wheel's libraries by construction, which is safer than a system toolkit of another version, but a torch built for CUDA 12 next to a stray cu13 wheel would pick cu13 first (layout order). Could be refined by preferring the major version of torch.version.cuda.
  • -l: syntax is GNU ld / lld / gold; not macOS (not a CUDA target) or MSVC (Windows is not supported by the JIT path today).
  • Driver lookup heuristics may miss unusual installs; OEQ_CUDA_DRIVER_DIR overrides.
  • Interaction with the existing stale-lock wait (_wait_for_torch_build_lock): unchanged.
